channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: Heavy fermions emerge at an atomic-layer interface, unlocking new ways to design quantum materials
item.description: A research team led by the University of Osaka has directly observed, for the first time, an unusual heavy-fermion state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. Such states are closely linked to exotic quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, and the finding opens new possibilities for designing quantum materials through their interfaces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Popular TikTok docs have big influence on Gen Z followers, new research finds
item.description: Young adults following physicians on TikTok consider them more accessible, credible and altruistic than their own doctors, even when the physician-influencers are selling products. Moreover, the followers haven't actually confirmed the influencers' medical credentials. Those are the main findings of a new study from Virginia Commonwealth University, co-authored by Suzanne Makarem, Ph.D., and published in the Journal of Consumer Affairs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Where are the best places for life in the cosmos? A universe in a supercomputer yields an answer
item.description: Earth seems like a troubled place right now, but at least our cosmic surroundings appear peaceful. This is not universally true, as explosions, collisions and other dangers lurk in other places and times. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: To keep GPS constellations from drifting, look to the moon
item.description: Global positioning systems are a key feature in everyday life for much of the world's population. Whether it's ensuring a ship delivers its goods safely or helping you avoid a road closure on your commute home, GPS can help. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warming oceans reshape plankton, potentially leaving fish with less nutritious food
item.description: The world is changing. As humans, we tend to focus on what happens on land, but the planet's food systems depend on both terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A symbiotic marketplace: Gutless worms swap essential bacterial partners over time
item.description: A typical scene at a local farmers market: Various stalls offer fruit, vegetables and much more. Every customer has their favorite stalls, though these may change occasionally. Some symbiotic relationships seem to work just like that, a study by researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology reveals in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How political, cultural, and economic forces can shape the risk of zoonotic disease
item.description: In eastern Ethiopia, pressures like conflict and displacement are changing how people and their camels travel, shifting livestock into new environments and potentially influencing the risk of zoonotic diseases spreading between animals and humans. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese team creates ‘lifelike’ hydrogel that changes shape for smart devices
item.description: Chinese researchers have developed a “lifelike” shape-changing hydrogel they say could provide a platform for next-generation developments, such as flexible tissue engineering scaffolds, brain-computer interfaces and humanlike robots. Inspired by living organisms, the team created a light-triggered system called STERS, which uses liquid metal particles to generate slow, self-sustaining chemical reactions that allow a hydrogel to change its structure over time. Capable of growing and changing... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Can a passing black hole disturbance leave a trace in Hawking radiation?
item.description: Black holes, despite their extreme nature, are described by surprisingly few basic parameters: their mass, charge and spin. Two black holes may have formed for completely different reasons and passed through very different histories, yet still end up in the same final state. John Wheeler summarized this idea with the famous phrase "black holes have no hair." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacteria use collisions to navigate crowded environments, micro-maze experiments reveal
item.description: Some bacteria can sense when they bump into each other and use these interactions to shape how the group organizes and moves. This discovery reveals a new way microbes explore their environments using physical feedback rather than chemical signals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI chatbots may increase accurate political knowledge
item.description: As voters seeking information about political issues increasingly turn to LLMs to do research, will AI lead them astray with hallucinations and bias, distorting the democratic process? Maybe not, according to a study of AI use in the 2024 U.K. election, published in PNAS Nexus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular complexity as a signature of life
item.description: An abundance of complex molecules has been proposed as a universal signature of life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Colorectal cancer is rising in young people and often found too late
item.description: Colorectal cancer in young people is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, with researchers finding most patients age 21 or younger already had Stage III or IV disease. Because symptoms like rectal bleeding, weight loss, abdominal pain, and bowel changes may be overlooked, researchers are calling for greater vigilance. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Vanillin provides a sweet solution for chronic wound healing
item.description: A team from Flinders University's Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties, making it a good candidate for wound-healing formulations. Their work is published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fasting is a common practice, whether for religious reasons or with the goal of losing weight, preventing chronic disease, or even slowing aging. Those who fast for hea... Ver más
item.description: Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
item.description: Scientists have found a surprising way to regrow damaged knee cartilage by blocking a protein that becomes more abundant with age. In old mice, the treatment restored naturally lost cartilage and also helped prevent osteoarthritis after ACL-like knee injuries, while human cartilage taken from knee replacement patients began producing new, functional joint cartilage after exposure to the same inhibitor. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Blue light could cut food poisoning from raw chicken
item.description: A low-power blue light could be the key to significantly reducing food poisoning caused by raw chicken in the U.K., scientists at the University of Reading have found. Campylobacter is the most common cause of bacterial food poisoning worldwide. In the U.K. alone, there are hundreds of thousands of cases each year, costing an estimated £700 million annually in health care and lost productivity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Counting purpose and connection could reveal overlooked benefits of bike paths and parks
item.description: It's often the sight of heavy digging machinery that makes us question how our taxes and property taxes are being spent. As a new project begins, we may wonder why money is being spent on that and not on other things. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Webb Captures Commotion From Nebula’s Stellar Jets
item.description: A cauldron of cosmic creation is being revealed in a new image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. Webb has unveiled numerous stars formerly hidden by clouds of dust in a stellar nursery known as NGC 7129, which resides about 3,300 light-years from Earth. Stars, the engines of elemental creation, have life cycles that begin […] Publicado también por: European Space Agency. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
item.description: Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New report exposes modern poverty and inequality in one of Britain's 'most affluent cities'
item.description: The University of York's Cost of Living Research Group has examined modern living standards across the city and revealed the extent of hidden pockets of poverty and inequality in one of the North's most affluent cities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists say this simple habit could strengthen your marriage
item.description: Couples who exercise together report better communication, healthier conflict resolution, and lower marital stress than those who work out alone. Even something as simple as taking a walk together may create valuable opportunities to talk, listen, and feel more connected. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Africa's rhinos often get the spotlight—but Indonesia's two rhino species are far closer to extinction
item.description: Small, hairy and cheekily charismatic. Those words sprang to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) after traversing the maze of wooden slat paths at the conservation center in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US, German scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on light and brain
item.description: American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine ​on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain. Publicado también por: The Washington Post - World. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
item.description: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Yosemite's meadows can be restored, but it will take time and effort
item.description: Researchers at Colorado State University are leading an attempt to restore Yosemite National Park's iconic meadows before it's too late by reintroducing native plants that once covered the landscape. Results are published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Un pueblo zamorano de 180 habitantes quería decorar sus calles así que sus vecinas tejieron 15 metros de ganchillo
item.description: El ganchillo (el de verdad, no el de la IA ) siempre fue un pasatiempo de calma y tiempo libre. Salvo cuando un pueblo entero se junta y decide convertirlo en parte de la festividad. Si en tu pueblo la fiesta empieza con traca y cohetes, en Losacino de Alba, en la zamorana Tierra de Alba, la fiesta empezó con una aguja. Del 2 al 4 de octubre, por la Virgen del Rosario, sus calles se vistieron con 20 hilos, más de 150 metros de cuerda y unos 300 banderines de ganchillo , muchos de mandalas y espirales. Las vecinas los tejieron durante meses y los jóvenes los colgaron. Cómo se teje una fiesta… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Isra Fdez

item.title: One simple addition to postpartum care made a major difference
item.description: New mothers paired with patient navigators were much more likely to receive postpartum care, depression screening, preventive testing, and ongoing primary care. By helping with barriers such as transportation, childcare, scheduling, and confusing medical information, navigators may provide a powerful way to improve women’s long-term health. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel
item.description: Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space. Fuente: BBC News - World.

item.title: Cancer survival is improving, but return‑to‑work support is falling behind
item.description: Australia has made significant strides in improving cancer survival, but new research from Griffith University finds far less progress in supporting survivors' return to work, which remains a major challenge for many. The industry research report, "Return-to-Work for Cancer Survivors in the Life Insurance Context," was a joint research collaboration between Griffith University and Hannover Life Re of Australasia Ltd. and was published in the Griffith Research Repository. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SpaceX desafía décadas de superstición de la NASA y lanza con éxito una misión tripulada con el número 13
item.description: Las supersticiones pueden arraigarse muchísimo con el paso de los años. Igual que la supuesta muerte de Molière tras vestir de amarillo en una representación teatral en 1673 ha llevado a que hoy en día nadie use ese color en los escenarios, la explosión de un tanque de oxígeno en la nave del Apolo 13 condujo a que ninguna misión estadounidense llevase como apellido ese número de mal agüero. Al menos no hasta ahora, pues la misión Crew-13 de SpaceX lo ha lucido sin miedo y ha llegado a su destino con éxito. Rápidos y superando miedos . Desde lo ocurrido con el Apolo 13, la carrera espacial… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: New report reveals gaps in corporate modern slavery disclosures
item.description: Many of Australia's largest companies fail to show enough public evidence that workers affected by modern slavery can safely report concerns, a new Monash University–led report has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Race With U.S., China Struggles to Recruit Foreign A.I. Researchers
item.description: China’s booming artificial intelligence sector has given local researchers good reason to remain in the country, but it has yet to lure overseas scientists despite a government push. Fuente: The New York Times - World.
item.dc:creator: Zeyi Yang

item.title: Nature's capacity to 'bounce back' when species are lost is vastly overestimated, global analysis finds
item.description: The idea that ecosystems carry plenty of backup, so if a small number of species become extinct there is little harm, has been greatly overestimated, according to the largest global study of its kind. Publicado también por: Hacker News - Portada. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European rover trains for Mars in the desert
item.description: For eight days, a Mars rover prototype travelled 220 metres across a barren landscape, following commands from a science team some 1200 kilometres away. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Scientists finally see how nature moves energy so efficiently
item.description: Researchers have captured key steps in a chemical reaction that helps nature transfer energy with remarkable efficiency. Ultrafast X-rays revealed how changes involving electrons and protons are closely linked to the rearrangement of surrounding water molecules. Because similar reactions drive photosynthesis and other energy-conversion processes, the technique could help scientists develop better catalysts, fuel cells, and flow batteries. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?
item.description: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries. Now, new research offers an explanation for why a… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Philip Oltermann European culture editor

item.title: California scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
item.description: Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Switching on brain cells: The Nobel-winning science of optogenetics
item.description: The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the neuroscience field of optogenetics. In optogenetics, scientists control neurones by stimulating them with light -- potentially unlocking breakthroughs for conditions such as dementia, depression and blindness. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis reports. Publicado también por: France 24 - English. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Russia reports a worker at a Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from an unknown cause and died
item.description: Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an "unknown" cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week. Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dos alemanes y un estadounidense ganan premio Nobel de Medicina por su trabajo en optogenética
item.description: Las investigaciones del psiquiatra y neurólogo estadounidense Karl Deisseroth y de sus colegas alemanes Peter Hegemann y Georg Nagel fueron las galardonadas con el Premio Nobel de Medicina por su trabajo en la optogenética. Los descubrimientos de los tres científicos podrían aportar información valiosa para futuros tratamientos para trastornos neurológicos y sensoriales, como la enfermedad de Parkinson y la epilepsia. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: A few drops of this Japanese tree oil may help you sleep more soundly
item.description: In a small study, sleeping near the scent of Hinoki root essential oil was linked to fewer nighttime awakenings, better morning alertness, and brain-wave changes associated with smoother sleep onset. The findings suggest an overlooked forestry byproduct could someday become a natural ingredient in sleep and relaxation products. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: En Japón, una oscura superstición sigue clasificando a sus ciudadanos por un atributo genético: su grupo sanguíneo
item.description: "No creo en el horóscopo, pero". Es la típica idea que podemos oírle a mucha de la gente a nuestro alrededor, e incluso muchos de nosotros nos reconocemos un poco en esas descripciones más o menos generales que nos definen según nuestros signos zodiacales. En varios de los trabajos en los que he estado había alguien que cogía el periódico y le echaba un vistazo a las predicciones de los tarotistas sobre lo que iba a pasarle esa semana. Pero, al parecer, los japoneses pueden ganarnos en supersticiones absurdas. Uno de los países más desarrollados intelectual y tecnológicamente del planeta… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: Dissolved organic matter and suspended sediment mingle in the southernmost extent of James Bay. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Tropical trees built homes for ants. Wasps are taking them over
item.description: Predatory wasps are hijacking shelters built by tropical trees for their ant defenders, potentially disrupting an ancient partnership that protects the plants from hungry insects. The takeover is far more common in disturbed landscapes such as oil palm plantations and could have lasting consequences for forest recovery and evolution. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Carefree shoppers most likely to receive retail discounts, study finds
item.description: Research involving Durham University Business School reveals how retailers target customers most likely to spend more. Shoppers who take a more carefree approach to spending are more likely to receive personalized discount codes from retailers, according to the research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Exploring systemic racism as the default explanation for disparities
item.description: Much of the field of sociology treats systemic racism as its default explanation for racial disparities rather than as an open question that requires further investigation and evidence, according to a recent position paper. The assumptions and moralization surrounding the origins of race-based disparities have undermined the discipline and made it difficult—and professionally costly—to challenge the concept, says author Ilana Redstone, a professor of sociology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vitamin B1 gains in wild lake trout embryos challenge assumptions drawn from hatcheries
item.description: For decades, fisheries managers have struggled to restore recruitment in wild lake trout populations across the Great Lakes region, with limited success. Returning this species to its former abundance is hampered by overfishing, sea lamprey predation, invasive species and habitat alterations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Neutrons, rotating black holes, and a galactic PeVatron at the center of the Milky Way
item.description: Galactic black holes are cosmic mitochondria, powerhouses of the universe. Most of the energy these supermassive black holes produce comes from the material surrounding them: superheated plasma in their accretion disks interacting with tremendous magnetic fields. But there is a more direct way to extract energy from a black hole. It's known as the Penrose process, and a new study asks whether we could discover a signature of this process. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MIT scientists find a hidden cancer risk of the keto diet
item.description: A ketogenic diet increased small-intestinal tumors in cancer-prone mice while reducing tumors in the colon, revealing a strikingly different response within neighboring parts of the gut. Researchers traced the increased risk not to ketones, but to the way intestinal stem cells processed the diet’s high levels of fat. That fat-burning activity pushed the cells to multiply more rapidly, potentially raising the chance of cancerous changes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 26 mil reproducciones · 330 reacciones | Nos EUA - Um brasileiro de 46 anos foi preso no último domingo (4) após aparecer vestido como um agente do Serviço de Imigração e Controle de Alfândegas dos Estados Unidos (ICE, na sigla em inglês) em um local de votação das eleições brasileiras Miami, na Flórida. ➡️​ Segundo o gabinete do xerife do condado de Miami-Dade, Danilo Silva circulava pelo campus de Kendall do Miami Dade College, onde brasileiros votavam, usando boné e jaqueta com identificação do ICE, óculos escuros, máscara cobrindo o rosto e botas táticas. De acordo com o relatório policial, ele caminhava pelos locais de votação e abordava pessoas na intenção de causar medo entre os eleitores. A NBC filmou o momento da prisão. Após receber as denúncias, agentes uniformizados e investigadores à paisana passaram a monitorar a área. Em determinado momento, Silva foi confrontado por dois homens, um deles filmando a situação. Os envolvidos iniciaram uma discussão, e os investigadores intervieram. Questionado pelos policiais, Silva admitiu que não era agente federal. Segundo o relato, ele afirmou que as roupas eram uma "fantasia" comprada pela internet, na Amazon. Ainda de acordo com as autoridades, o homem disse que havia comparecido ao local para votar usando uma camisa da seleção brasileira. Depois, retornou ao carro, trocou de roupa e vestiu o uniforme semelhante ao utilizado por agentes do ICE. Aos investigadores, Silva afirmou que queria apenas "ver a reação das pessoas". ➡️​ Ele foi preso em flagrante. Segundo o relatório da polícia, durante a abordagem, ele ficou exaltado e ameaçou um dos investigadores, dizendo que ele se arrependeria da decisão de prendê-lo. Segundo o Miami Herald, em seguida, Silva tentou subornar os policiais para ser liberado. De acordo com o jornal, ele ofereceu dinheiro e disse que poderia mostrar a transferência pelo celular. Ele foi levado para o centro de detenção Turner Guilford Knight. Ele foi acusado de intimidação de eleitores, tentativa de suborno, uso ilegal de insígnias das forças de segurança e conduta desordeira. Saiba mais no #g1. #ice #brasileiro #estadosunidos #notícias #g1mundo | g1 - O Portal de Notícias da globo

item.description: Written by Alex Jones, Ph.D. candidate at Imperial College London Sept. 29, 2026 After spending the last six months exploring “Lac de Charmes,” a region of ancient rock beyond Jezero crater’s western rim, Perseverance has stumbled upon a vast field of light-toned rocks peppering the Martian surface. Light-colored rocks are a strange sight on Mars, […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Global soil erosion outpaces natural recovery, report warns
item.description: Isaac Larsen, an associate professor in the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, is a lead author of "Status of the World's Soil Resources 2026," a new report produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) that draws on recent scientific literature and contributions from hundreds of experts around the world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political orientation and institutional trust emerge as key factors in local wind energy support
item.description: Why does the expansion of wind energy sometimes meet with local resistance, even though renewable energy generally enjoys broad support? RIFS researcher Jörg Radtke used a representative survey of 6,284 people in North Rhine-Westphalia to investigate which social characteristics are linked to the acceptance of wind energy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Game simulator shows how math can guide decisions when resources are limited
item.description: In "Bloons Tower Defense," the goal is to stop balloons from reaching the end of a track by strategically placing towers along the route. These towers vary in cost, range and attack power, and they also take up valuable space. The game becomes increasingly difficult with each round. Where you place a tower therefore determines not only how effective it is now but also which options remain available later in the game. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flu season could kick off ‘incredibly’ early — what scientists are watching
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03150-8 Cases in the Northern Hemisphere are cropping up weeks early, and they are dominated by a virus with a concerning mutation. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03092-1 Francis Halzen wins the 2026 award for his work on a neutrino observatory at the South Pole that has helped to unlock mysteries of the Universe. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Davide Castelvecchi

item.title: Brain organoids grafted into cortex-free mice will advance human brain research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02967-7 Cell-based models of the human cortex transplanted into mice produce neurons that are inaccessible in vitro, and could enable scientists to link brain injury to behaviour. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Aparna Bhaduri

item.title: 'Digital ibuprofen' offers Chinese youth comfort through cute characters facing familiar struggles
item.description: In China, young people are encountering a myriad of challenges, from societal pressures around success to life in a highly surveilled society, that have led them to turn to the internet in search of a balm to soothe their pain. What has emerged is a host of content called "digital ibuprofen"—viewed as a way to numb the anxieties of modern living. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Attention can't be bought, so brands turn to memes
item.description: The funniest post you saw this week may not have come from a friend; it may have come from a brand. Whether it is Kohl's, Wendy's, or Netflix, brands are behaving more like internet users than traditional advertisers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unusual senses: The secret superpowers of amphibians and reptiles
item.description: The Surinam toad is one of the strangest frogs on Earth. Flat-bodied, tiny-eyed and adapted to the murky waters of the Amazon basin, it hunts well despite having very poor vision. When a fish swims close, the frog suddenly opens its mouth and sucks the prey inside in a fraction of a second. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What a locust can teach us about how neuromodulators alter odor processing
item.description: When you walk into a bakery and smell fresh cookies, the enticing smell draws you in. After you eat a handful of cookies, though, the same smell likely doesn't send you back for more. Researchers in the McKelvey School of Engineering at Washington University in St. Louis sought to determine the biological mechanisms in the brain that controllably alters odor-evoked behavior by using an unlikely model—a locust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rhinos and elephants can cause huge problems if reintroduced badly—here's how to get it right
item.description: Moving large animals around is a seductive idea in conservation. If there are plenty of animals in one place and too few in another, moving some between the two seems an obvious solution. Sometimes it is. But with animals as large, mobile and socially complicated as elephants and rhinos, the move itself can turn out to be the straightforward part. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Budding rocket scientists put designs to the test in outback competition
item.description: Domestic and international students turn a remote sheep station into a testing ground for their designs as they compete in the Australian Universities Rocket Competition. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Bill Ormonde and Sarah McConnell

item.title: D’Arros shearwater colony grew nearly 10-fold after rats were eradicated
item.description: D'Arros Island's Wedge-tailed Shearwater population rose dramatically after rats were eradicated in 2003. Researchers recorded 2,768 breeding pairs in 2016 and 2,406 pairs in 2021. The colony spread across a larger area and exhibited higher breeding burrow density during later surveys. The study utilized direct counts and area-based estimates to determine breeding pair numbers. Identifying the peak incubation period in November was crucial for future population comparisons. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Quantum interactions may have locked early universe's fields into existing energy states
item.description: The universe may be trapped in its own comfort zone, and a researcher in the College of Engineering and Computer Science has helped explain why it cannot seem to leave. A new study suggests the universe could be locked into its current state by the same kinds of quantum effects that scientists study when trying to preserve fragile information inside a quantum computer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Does increased childcare funding help mothers into work?
item.description: Since Labor won the 2024 general election, policy focused on children in the early years—from birth to school age—and their parents has moved sharply up the political agenda. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forests are dying along North Carolina's coast—and it's speeding up
item.description: A new study finds that coastal forest loss in North Carolina's Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula began accelerating after 2010 and may still be speeding up. The study also found that North Carolina lost more than 20% of its coastal forest between 1985 and 2021. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An iced coffee won't predict job performance—but it might reveal hiring bias
item.description: Imagine two candidates with identical qualifications interviewing for the same job. One arrives carrying a bottle of water, while the other walks in with an iced coffee. Should that difference matter? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Switching on brain cells: the Nobel-winning science of optogenetics
item.description: The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the neuroscience field of optogenetics. In optogenetics, scientists control neurones by stimulating them with light -- potentially unlocking breakthroughs for conditions such as dementia, depression and blindness. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis reports. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: NASA to Stream SpaceX Crew-12 Return, Splashdown Live
item.description: NASA and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 8:05 a.m. EDT, Wednesday, Oct. 7, for the undocking of the agency’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from the International Space Station, pending weather conditions. An Oct. 7 undock puts NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Rare insect discovery reveals a new species from the dinosaur age
item.description: Some 99 million years ago, during the age of the dinosaurs, a tiny insect belonging to a species previously unknown to science became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber, and the fossil preserved within it has now enabled a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describe a new species: Cretodorus noonoo, or "Noo-Noo." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How psychopathic traits shape language
item.description: Popular culture often depicts people with psychopathy as cold, emotionless and hollow, but a recent University of Mississippi study found that the language associated with psychopathic traits is more complicated than often described. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experts deem empowering neurologists and neurology trainees to perform lumbar punctures at bedside a worthwhile goal
item.description: Many medical specialties now require graduating doctors to be skilled in point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing patients and performing procedures. POCUS uses a portable ultrasound device to help clinicians make fast, accurate medical decisions. The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education lists this skill as an official milestone for graduation. Even though training is improving for its potential use in treating head, eye and nerve conditions, POCUS is only moderately used by neurologists dealing with some neurological conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA evidence narrows down when people first reached the Americas
item.description: One of the unresolved mysteries about the history of the Americas is when the first people arrived. Despite extensive debate centering on genetic, archaeological and environmental evidence, there is still no consensus or conclusive proof. Did they enter before, during or after the coldest period of the last ice age, known as the Last Glacial Maximum? Evidence from recent analysis of ancient DNA is providing fresh clues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Standard 3D printers let labs build and adapt tools for bacterial research
item.description: Studying microorganisms requires instruments with extremely high precision. Such instruments are expensive and take a long time to manufacture using traditional methods, which has slowed progress in the field. It has also been difficult for the biologists who use these instruments to participate directly in their development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronomers catch a star slowly snacking on a brown dwarf, 300 light years away
item.description: Like Earth, most planetary bodies circle their star in stable, detached orbits. These companionable systems can suddenly change when a planet comes too close to its star. In such a close encounter, a star can pull the planet in and swallow it whole. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How game publishers set international prices: A study reveals four pricing approaches on Steam
item.description: Although digital platforms make it possible to sell the same product globally, prices often vary across countries because of differences in purchasing power, currencies, taxation and other market conditions. At the same time, the transparency of online prices enables consumers to compare prices across regions easily. Companies therefore must balance local affordability with the need to avoid excessive international price differences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A health app designed for teachers
item.description: A new app is designed to help teachers stay healthy in their day-to-day work. The digital tool is the result of a three-year collaborative project between the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and health insurance provider AOK Bayern. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atomic motion could help push solar cells beyond conventional limits
item.description: The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE), a photoelectric effect that generates photocurrent without a p–n junction, can persist even when a material's average crystal structure remains centrosymmetric, a study from Institute of Science Tokyo has found. Researchers demonstrated this in CuCrP2S6, a van der Waals material that transitions from a noncentrosymmetric to a centrosymmetric average structure. The finding challenges the conventional view of BPVE and suggests a new strategy for enhancing photoelectric conversion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After losing her mother to MS, J.K. Rowling gave £10m to research
item.description: J.K. Rowling opened the Anne Rowling Regenerative Neurology Clinic in memory of her mother, who died of multiple sclerosis. The clinic focuses on research and treatment of various neurological diseases, including multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease. The funding aims to attract world-class researchers to develop new therapies and potentially find a cure. It has already hosted numerous clinical appointments and research projects since its inception. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Quantum systems never quite forget where they came from
item.description: Even the most chaotic quantum systems keep a permanent mark of their own past—a "quantum birthmark"—that never fades. Researchers from Tampere University, Harvard University and TU Dresden discovered the feature in their recent study. Their findings shed new light on the elusive relationship between classical and quantum mechanics. Looking ahead, these quantum birthmarks, along with related phenomena known as "scars," could eventually be harnessed to power next-generation nanoelectronics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unmowed strips attract insects, but many abandon partially mowed dikes
item.description: Municipalities are increasingly mowing dikes and verges in stages, so that insects can make longer use of the plants growing there. Mowing is essential to keep a dike strong, explains ecologist Constant Swinkels of Radboud University. "If you don't mow, trees or sturdy shrubs such as blackberries may start to grow. You don't want that, because their roots are so thick that they can cause dikes to collapse." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A novel path to fusion ignition: Heat first, then add fuel
item.description: For more than 70 years, fusion energy researchers have used a particular equation to judge whether a plasma would stay hot and dense enough—for long enough—to reach a point where it could sustain itself without any more external power added. While that equation marks the finish line, also known as ignition, it says nothing about the best way to reach it. New research from the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) maps a path to ignition conditions using far less energy than any other path. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sniffer dogs, bloodstain patterns and ballistics evidence under the microscope in new studies
item.description: CSI may have spawned innumerable spinoffs, but it turns out you can't trust TV—or sniffer dogs. New research is questioning the scientific basis for the dogs' use by police, as well as aspects of bloodstain pattern analysis and ballistics evidence routinely used in courts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Florida Keys heat wave reveals nearly fourfold death risk for diseased coral
item.description: Disease and heat pose a deadly combination for coral reefs, according to a new University of Georgia study published in the journal Coral Reefs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Russia is using Ukraine's children to win its occupation—and the wider war
item.description: A year or so after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the city of Murmansk in Russia's Arctic northwest marked its annual regional day with a celebration for children. Alongside the sons and daughters of Russian soldiers stood children taken from the occupied Prymorskyi district of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Local tipping points in dune landscapes: How does a dune system organize itself?
item.description: Building with nature is an important concept in our coastal defense. After all, by harnessing natural processes, we are more resilient to sea level rise. A good understanding of these processes is therefore indispensable. Ecologist Paul Berghuis, affiliated with Utrecht University and the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ), delved into the world of dune formation and discovered that within young dune landscapes, dunes and grasses do not arrange themselves randomly but follow a fixed pattern. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Detecting forever chemicals—with yeast and AI
item.description: If you're reading this, your body probably contains forever chemicals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists found at least 10 likely new species of bizarre branching worms inside sea sponges
item.description: Researchers have identified ten likely new species of branching marine worms found within sea sponges. These unusual worms exhibit a unique tree-like body structure, which has evolved over time. Genetic analysis and museum specimens helped resolve the long-standing classification issues of these marine organisms. The study indicates these worms' diversification relates closely to their sponge hosts and geographic locations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: ESA at IAC 2026 – Day 1
item.description: Stronger European capabilities and deeper international cooperation were at the heart of ESA’s first day at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye. From exploration to the contribution of space to society, ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher underlined the importance of Europe becoming a stronger and more capable partner in a rapidly changing space environment. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: "Lo hice para vengar a Gaza, quería morir como mártir": el copiloto del vuelo de Flydubai confesó por qué atacó al piloto
item.description: Hammam Al-Hammami fue interrogado por los investigadores de Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Mientras, Israel busca determinar si el piloto actuó solo o si fue enviado por otra persona. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Tracking uncovers $80 million spent on AI political ads, most without disclosure
item.description: The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people's televisions and social media feeds. We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle—using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending—we've tracked about $80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sharks' inner ears reveal surprising diversity that may reflect evolution more than environment
item.description: A new study of shark anatomy suggests the shape of their inner ears is far more variable than expected, and this variation could have more to do with their evolutionary history than where they live or what they eat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why Great Plains rivers depend on wetlands as well as climate
item.description: When a prairie river carries more water in one year than another, the obvious place to look for an explanation is the sky. A year with more snow and rain should have more water in rivers. That was also how I initially thought about year-to-year changes in river flow. But while studying the Prairie Pothole Region, I learned that this is only part of the story. What happens after water reaches the ground can be just as important as how much falls from the sky. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controlling the brain with light earns a physiology Nobel
item.description: The entire field of optogenetics traces back to light-seeking algae. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.description: Imagine losing an arm and simply growing a new one. This amazing ability of regeneration isn't just something from a superhero movie—it actually happens in real life for some animals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pollen study reveals the hidden history of grasses
item.description: Scientists used machine learning and super-resolution microscopy to overcome a challenge that has stymied research into the natural history of grasses for decades. Their method allowed them to detect subtle differences among grass pollen grains and trace changes in grass diversity and the proportions of the two main photosynthetic types of grasses at one site over a period of 25,000 years. Fuente: Phys.org.
